Creating The Right Mood For a Performance; Series 2 What Experience Has Taught Me Over the years of performing, directing choirs, training singers, and working with musicians, I have learned something that may not be found in a music theory book: your emotional state can influence your performance just as much as your musical preparation. I remember occasions when I arrived at a performance venue technically prepared. I knew my songs, understood the arrangement, rehearsed with the team, and was confident that everything would go well. Yet, somehow, the performance did not feel as good as I expected. On other occasions, I have walked onto a stage after a difficult or stressful day, but something changed the moment the music began. I deliberately shifted my attention from whatever was happening around me to the purpose of the performance. My mind became calmer, my focus improved, and I was able to connect with the audience and the music. That experience taught me that being ready to perform is not only about knowing what to sing or play; it is also about being mentally and emotionally ready to perform. Your Mood Can Affect Your Performance A singer who is anxious may struggle with breathing, pitch, confidence, or expression. A musician who is distracted may miss cues or make mistakes. A choir that comes on stage carrying tension from rehearsals may sound technically correct but lack warmth and connection. This does not mean we must always feel happy before performing. That is unrealistic. Rather, we must learn how to manage our emotions and intentionally create the right performance mindset. Before I perform or lead a team, I try to ask myself: What is the purpose of this performance? What atmosphere do we want to create? What does the audience need from us? Those questions help me move my attention away from unnecessary distractions and toward the performance itself. The Right Mood Doesn’t Happen by Accident One thing experience has taught me is that the mood for a performance often begins before you get on stage. How you arrive at the venue matters. How you respond when something goes wrong during rehearsal matters. Even the conversation you have immediately before walking onto the stage can influence the atmosphere. This is why I encourage musicians and singers to avoid unnecessary arguments, negative conversations, panic, and last-minute confusion before performing. Take a moment | Breathe | Listen Pray or reflect, if appropriate. Review your first entry and important cues. Then remind yourself why you are there. Don’t Confuse Energy With Noise Having the right mood does not necessarily mean becoming excessively excited. Sometimes the best performance preparation is quiet. A singer may need a few minutes of silence before going on stage. A choir may need to gather together and mentally settle. A band may need to focus on communication rather than joking around immediately before a performance. The goal is not to manufacture an emotion. The goal is to create the emotional and mental space that allows you to perform at your best. Preparation Gives You Confidence I have also discovered that the right mood becomes much easier to achieve when you have prepared properly. It is difficult to feel calm when you don’t know your music. It is difficult to feel confident when you haven’t rehearsed your transitions. It is difficult to connect with your audience when you are still wondering what comes next. Good preparation reduces unnecessary anxiety. When you know your material, understand your role, trust your team, and have rehearsed possible challenges, you have more freedom to focus on expression and connection. The Performance Begins Before the First Note Today, I see performance preparation differently. The performance does not begin when the microphone is switched on or when the conductor raises his hands. It begins in your mind before you step onto the stage. Learn to leave unnecessary distractions behind. Learn to manage nervousness. Learn to encourage your team. Learn to understand the atmosphere you are trying to create. Because sometimes, the difference between an ordinary performance and a memorable one is not another rehearsal. Creating The Right Mood For a Performance; Series 1 Learning to Move Beyond Your Personal Feelings… A great performance is not only about singing the right notes, playing the right chords, or remembering the arrangement. It is also about creating and communicating the right emotional atmosphere. As singers, choristers and musicians, we sometimes arrive at a performance carrying emotions that have nothing to do with what we are about to perform. You may be tired, discouraged, worried about something happening at home, disappointed by something that happened during rehearsal, or simply not feeling energetic. Yet the audience is waiting. The music still needs to communicate. This is where professional emotional discipline becomes important. YOUR PERSONAL MOOD IS NOT ALWAYS THE MOOD OF THE PERFORMANCE. One of the most important lessons I have learned as a music director, music instructor, mentor, producer and voice coach is that how you feel personally and what the performance requires are not always the same thing. Imagine a singer who has had a difficult morning but is expected to lead a joyful worship song. Or a choir that has just experienced tension during rehearsal but needs to walk on stage and communicate unity and warmth. Or a saxophonist who is mentally distracted but has been assigned a powerful solo that requires confidence and energy. The challenge is not necessarily to pretend that your personal feelings don’t exist. The challenge is to recognize your emotional state, manage it, and deliberately enter the emotional world required by the music. Music Carries Emotion Music is more than sound. A melody can communicate joy. A minor progression can create sadness or tension. A rhythmic groove can create excitement. A slow musical passage can create reflection. A powerful crescendo can communicate anticipation, triumph or intensity. Therefore, performers must ask: “What should the audience feel when they hear this?” That question can change the way you perform. A singer shouldn’t simply sing the lyrics. They should understand the emotion behind them. A pianist shouldn’t simply play the notes. They should understand the character of the music. A drummer shouldn’t simply keep time. They should understand how rhythm contributes to the atmosphere. A choir shouldn’t simply sing together. They should communicate a collective emotional message. SOMETIMES YOU HAVE TO COME OUT OF YOUR MOOD… This does not mean suppressing your emotions or pretending to be someone you are not. It means developing the ability to transition emotionally. You might enter rehearsal feeling quiet and withdrawn, but the music requires energy. You might feel excited personally, but the piece requires calmness and sensitivity. You might be frustrated with something that happened before the performance, but the audience needs to experience peace, joy or confidence through your performance. Professional performers learn how to make this transition intentionally. Think of it as changing musical gears. You don’t remain in the same emotional gear throughout every performance. “A professional performer does not always perform from the mood they came with; they learn to enter the mood the music requires and invite the audience into it.”— Victor Adenola #art #band #bands #choir #churchchoir #EmotionalWellBeing #ImprovedDisciplineAndPatience #musicians #musicperformance #performance #performancetips #rehearsal #rehearsals #selfCare #singer #singers #singersgospelSingers #stagepresence #Victoradenola
